title: K-12 Special Education and Related Services Pay Benchmarks
metaTitle: School SLP, Special Ed and Para Pay by State, 2026
description: BLS pay for special education teachers, school SLPs, OTs, PTs, school psychologists and paraprofessionals: national medians, ranges and pay by state.
answer: In elementary and secondary schools, the May 2025 BLS median is $83,080 for speech-language pathologists, $85,610 for occupational therapists, $94,120 for school psychologists, $96,080 for physical therapists, $65,080 to $74,510 for special education teachers, $36,990 for teaching assistants and $20.62 an hour for short-term substitutes. For teachers, psychologists and aides, the top state pays about double the lowest.
keyTakeaways: In elementary and secondary schools, the May 2025 BLS median is $83,080 for speech-language pathologists and $94,120 for school psychologists.
Schools pay speech-language pathologists $14,790 less at the median than all employers do: $83,080 against $97,870.
School psychologist medians range from $127,780 in California to $61,070 in Mississippi, more than double from top to bottom.
Inside Pennsylvania, the SLP median is $100,080 in the Philadelphia metro and $64,010 in the Northwestern Pennsylvania nonmetropolitan area.
Wages and salaries are 61.2% of state and local government compensation costs, so a salary line leaves out 38.8% of what an employed seat costs (BLS, June 2026).
bodyHtml:
What do special education and related services roles earn nationally?

Related services clinicians earn $83,080 to $96,080 at the median in schools, and special education teachers earn $65,080 to $74,510 depending on grade band. Teaching assistants and short-term substitutes earn under $43,000. The table gives the 10th percentile, the median and the 90th percentile for each role in elementary and secondary schools, the industry BLS publishes for all 10 occupations, with the all-employer median beside it. The figures are the May 2025 estimates of the Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics survey, released May 15, 2026 (source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, OEWS program page).

The preschool, middle school and secondary rows come from the 25-2051, 25-2057 and 25-2058 profiles (source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, OEWS May 2025, OEWS May 2025 data tables).

Four things the national table tells you

  • Schools pay clinicians less than other employers do. The school median for speech-language pathologists is $83,080 against $97,870 across all employers, and home health care services pay a median of $117,370 (source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, OEWS May 2025, OEWS May 2025 data tables). Occupational therapists show the same pattern: $85,610 in schools, $100,330 overall (source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, OEWS May 2025, OEWS May 2025 data tables). Your SLP candidate is weighing your offer against those numbers.
  • School psychologists are the exception. Schools employ 53,670 of the 63,940 school psychologists BLS counts, so the school median ($94,120) sits close to the all-employer median ($95,990) (source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, OEWS May 2025, OEWS May 2025 data tables).
  • Special education teacher pay is set almost entirely by schools. Of 260,870 kindergarten and elementary special education teachers, 258,680 work in elementary and secondary schools (source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, OEWS May 2025, OEWS May 2025 data tables). Your salary schedule and your neighbors' schedules are the market.
  • Paraprofessionals are the largest group by far. Schools employ 1,185,500 of the 1,420,350 teaching assistants in the BLS count. The BLS code 25-9045 includes the 2018 occupation 25-9043, Teaching Assistants, Special Education, so it covers the 1:1 aides and instructional assistants in your special education program (source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, OEWS May 2025, OEWS May 2025 data tables).

Read the annual figures the way BLS builds them. For teachers and teaching assistants, BLS reports annual salaries only, because those roles do not generally work year-round, full time. For clinicians and substitutes, BLS publishes hourly wages and calculates the annual figure by multiplying by 2,080 hours (source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, OEWS May 2025, OEWS May 2025 data tables). That matters most for substitutes: the school median is $20.62 an hour, and few substitutes work 2,080 hours in a year. The hourly medians in schools are $39.94 for speech-language pathologists, $41.16 for occupational therapists, $46.19 for physical therapists and $45.25 for school psychologists (source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, OEWS May 2025, OEWS May 2025 data tables). For the cost of a seat that stays open, see what an unfilled classroom costs a district.

What do these roles pay in your state?

State medians run from $50,380 to $101,120 for special education teachers across the two grade bands and from $65,680 to $118,970 for speech-language pathologists, so your state's number is the one to use. BLS publishes state estimates across all employers, not for schools alone, so these tables use the all-employer median for each state (source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, OEWS May 2025, OEWS May 2025 data tables). The first 8 rows are the states FocusedEDU serves most. The next 10 are among the largest other states.

What stands out in the Mid-Atlantic and Southeast

  • New Jersey pays above Pennsylvania in every role shown. The median speech-language pathologist earns $101,560 in New Jersey and $92,960 in Pennsylvania. Secondary special education teachers earn $83,770 and $77,000.
  • The District of Columbia has the highest median in the country for kindergarten and elementary special education teachers, $97,910, and the second highest for teaching assistants, $46,920.
  • Maryland's school psychologist median of $109,700 is the fourth highest of any state.
  • Delaware's speech-language pathologist median, $102,760, is above the national all-employer median of $97,870.
  • North Carolina sits at the other end. Its secondary special education teacher median, $56,770, is among the five lowest, and its teaching assistant median is $29,790.

If you are filling special education classrooms in any of these states, the special education staffing page lists the roles and states FocusedEDU covers.

California and Washington rank among the five highest states for all five roles below, and Mississippi ranks among the five lowest for all five. For school psychologists, California's median of $127,780 is more than double Mississippi's $61,070. The table ranks the 50 states and the District of Columbia by median for each role.

Metropolitan and rural pay inside one state

The state median hides a second gap. BLS also publishes estimates for metropolitan areas and for nonmetropolitan areas, its term for the rural parts of each state. Inside Pennsylvania, the median speech-language pathologist earns $100,080 in the Philadelphia-Camden-Wilmington metro area and $64,010 in the Northwestern Pennsylvania nonmetropolitan area (source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, OEWS May 2025, OEWS May 2025 data tables). In North Carolina, the school psychologist median is $83,340 in Raleigh-Cary and $58,910 in both the Central and Western North Carolina nonmetropolitan areas (source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, OEWS May 2025, OEWS May 2025 data tables). The kindergarten and elementary special education teacher median is $91,610 in New York-Newark-Jersey City and $47,280 in Central North Carolina's nonmetropolitan area (source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, OEWS May 2025, OEWS May 2025 data tables). For teaching assistants, the Washington-Arlington-Alexandria metro median is $46,200 and Central North Carolina's nonmetropolitan median is $28,030 (source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, OEWS May 2025, OEWS May 2025 data tables).

Rural does not always mean lower. The Northern West Virginia nonmetropolitan area's speech-language pathologist median, $107,880, is above New York-Newark-Jersey City's $107,860 (source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, OEWS May 2025, OEWS May 2025 data tables).

Why the geography changes your search

A candidate compares your offer with the pay in the area where they live, not with a national average. Three consequences follow from the BLS figures:

  • An offer built on the national school median can miss the local market. A district near Philadelphia that offers the national school SLP median of $83,080 is $17,000 under the metro median.
  • Clinicians have outside options schools do not set. Home health care services and skilled nursing facilities pay speech-language pathologists more than schools do, so your search for a school-based SLP competes with them.
  • The same license pays very differently a few hours apart. Inside Pennsylvania, BLS shows a $36,070 gap in the SLP median between the Philadelphia metro and the Northwestern Pennsylvania nonmetropolitan area. A rural district paying its local median is recruiting against that gap.

Hard-to-fill clinical roles are covered on the related services staffing page.

Why is a contract rate not the same number as a salary?

A salary is only part of what your district spends on an employed seat, and a contract rate covers costs that never appear on a salary line. In June 2026, wages and salaries were 61.2% of employer compensation costs for state and local government workers, and benefits were the other 38.8%. Total compensation averaged $66.45 per hour worked, of which $40.67 was wages and $25.78 was benefits (source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Employer Costs for Employee Compensation, June 2026 release, September 9, 2026). In private industry, benefits were 30.0% (source: BLS ECEC, June 2026).

So when a business manager sets a contracted hourly rate next to a salary divided by hours, the comparison starts with more than a third of the public-sector cost missing. An hourly rate for a contracted professional covers things a salary line does not:

  • The district's own benefit and pension costs. The 38.8% share above sits on your books for every employed seat. For a contracted seat, it does not.
  • Recruiting. Posting, sourcing, screening and interviewing, which your HR office otherwise does in-house for every opening.
  • Credentialing. License and certification verification for the discipline, criminal background checks and the state clearances your state requires, completed before the first day.
  • Coverage for absences. When a contracted professional is out, finding the replacement is the agency's job, not your principal's.
  • Hours worked, not a contract year. A salary pays for the whole contract year. A contract rate is paid for the hours the seat is filled.
  • A clean exit or a permanent hire. If the need ends, the seat ends. If you want to keep the professional, a temp-to-perm conversion turns the seat into your hire.

The fair comparison is the contracted rate against the full cost of an employed seat, plus the cost of the seat staying empty while you search. The education staffing agency cost page walks through that comparison for districts.

How do you use pay data to set a competitive offer or a rate ceiling?

Start from the BLS figure for your exact role and your own area, then choose where on the range you need to sit. The steps below are practice, the way districts commonly put public pay data to work.

  1. Match the role to the right BLS code. A grade 3 autism support teacher is 25-2052. A 1:1 aide is a teaching assistant, 25-9045. A day-to-day substitute is 25-3031. Use the school industry figure for the national view, and remember that state and area figures cover all employers.
  2. Use your state and your area, not the nation. Look up the metro or nonmetropolitan area your candidates live in. The gap inside one state can be larger than the gap between states.
  3. For clinicians, check the all-employer figure too. The school median for speech-language pathologists sits $14,790 below the all-employer median, and that is the gap you recruit across.
  4. Pick a percentile on purpose. For a role with few applicants, aim above the median. Across all employers, the 75th percentile is $114,570 for speech-language pathologists, $120,310 for school psychologists, $80,280 for kindergarten and elementary special education teachers and $45,360 for teaching assistants (source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, OEWS May 2025, OEWS May 2025 data tables), (source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, OEWS May 2025, OEWS May 2025 data tables), (source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, OEWS May 2025, OEWS May 2025 data tables), (source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, OEWS May 2025, OEWS May 2025 data tables).
  5. Place the number on your salary schedule. Find the step and lane that reach it. If none does, that is the case to bring to your board.
  6. Set a contract ceiling against full cost. Price an employed seat at salary plus your own benefit and pension load (at the state and local average, about 63% of salary), then add what the open seat costs you each week it sits empty. That total, not the salary alone, is the ceiling to compare against.

A planning example: a district near Philadelphia needs a school-based speech-language pathologist. The national school median is $83,080. The Pennsylvania median is $92,960, and the Philadelphia-Camden-Wilmington metro median is $100,080 (source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, OEWS May 2025, OEWS May 2025 data tables). An offer at the national school figure starts $17,000 below what a local SLP earns at the median, which is why the search stalls. An offer near $100,080 is competitive. A contract ceiling for coverage while the search runs should be set against that salary plus the district's own benefit costs. In state and local government, benefits average $25.78 an hour for every $40.67 in wages, about 63% on top of salary, or roughly $63,400 on a $100,080 salary (source: BLS ECEC, June 2026) (source: BLS ECEC, June 2026).

Districts comparing ways to cover an open seat can read the paraprofessional staffing and substitute teacher staffing pages for how those roles are filled.

faqs.q: What is the school SLP salary, nationally and by state?
faqs.a: In elementary and secondary schools, the BLS median for speech-language pathologists was $83,080 a year in May 2025, or $39.94 an hour. The 10th percentile was $59,620 and the 90th was $130,270. Across all employers the median was $97,870, so schools pay below hospitals, home health and nursing facilities. By state, California had the highest median, $118,970.

faqs.q: What is the median special education teacher salary by state?
faqs.a: The May 2025 BLS medians for kindergarten and elementary special education teachers ranged from $97,910 in the District of Columbia to $50,380 in West Virginia. Secondary special education teachers ranged from $101,120 in Washington to $51,970 in Mississippi. Nationally, the school median was $65,080 for kindergarten and elementary and $74,510 for secondary. BLS reports these roles as annual salaries only.

faqs.q: How much do school psychologists make?
faqs.a: The median school psychologist in elementary and secondary schools earned $94,120 in May 2025, according to BLS. Schools employ 53,670 of the 63,940 school psychologists BLS counts, so the all-employer median, $95,990, is close. State medians run from $127,780 in California to $61,070 in Mississippi. Maryland, at $109,700, is fourth highest.

faqs.q: What do paraprofessionals and 1:1 aides make?
faqs.a: BLS counts paraprofessionals as teaching assistants, code 25-9045, which includes special education teaching assistants. The May 2025 median in elementary and secondary schools was $36,990, with a 10th percentile of $26,950 and a 90th of $50,850. Washington has the highest state median, $49,120, and Alabama the lowest, $24,070. Schools employ 1,185,500 of them.

faqs.q: How much do substitute teachers make per hour?
faqs.a: The median short-term substitute in elementary and secondary schools earned $20.62 an hour in May 2025, and $20.03 across all employers, according to BLS. BLS converts that hourly pay to an annual figure by multiplying by 2,080 hours, which few substitutes work, so the hourly number is the one to compare. State medians are highest in Alaska and California.

faqs.q: How much of a public-sector worker's cost is salary?
faqs.a: In June 2026, wages and salaries were 61.2% of employer compensation costs for state and local government workers, and benefits were 38.8%, according to the BLS Employer Costs for Employee Compensation release. Total compensation averaged $66.45 per hour worked. When you compare a contracted rate with a salary, add your own benefit and pension costs to the salary first.

faqs.a: Tell FocusedEDU the role and your state through the staffing request form, and FocusedEDU replies with the rate range for that role. You can also book a 30-minute call.
